988.title: The priest and the big bang
988.hook: Georges Lemaître, a Belgian priest and physicist, proposed the expanding universe
988.howItsDone: Christians hold a range of views on how scripture and science fit together; the Catholic Church has its own academy of sciences, and Christians work as scientists across many fields.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Laudato si', a pope's letter that opened with a song, and your line was our common home.

A man in a black clerical collar stands at a blackboard covered in equations. He's a Catholic priest, and also a physicist, trained in the mathematics of Einstein's theory of gravity. And the equations are telling him something strange. The universe isn't standing still. It's getting bigger. Run the film backward, he reasons, and everything gets closer and closer together, until it all begins from one small, dense starting point. He called it a primeval atom. Other people later gave it a nickname, and the nickname stuck. His name was Georges Lemaître, a Belgian priest.

The first line of the Bible, in the King James translation: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." A few lines later: "And God said, Let there be light: and there was light." It would be easy to hear Lemaître's idea, a universe with a beginning, and say: Genesis, proved by physics. Lemaître himself didn't want anyone to say that. When church voices began to treat his theory as scientific proof of creation, he pushed back, quietly but firmly. His reasoning, as it's usually reported: physics describes how the universe unfolds; it can't tell you whether there is a God. And the Bible wasn't written to teach science; it was written to teach the way to salvation. Keep the two in their own lanes, and neither has to be afraid of the other. He spent his life in both. He said Mass and did mathematics, and didn't think he was being torn in half. Christians have held a range of views on faith and science, and still do. Some read Genesis as a literal account of how the world was made. Others read it as a different kind of truth, about who made the world and why. Lemaître's own path was to study the heavens as closely as he could, and to keep praying. An old psalm sits well beside his blackboard: "The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork." The psalm doesn't do the math. It looks up, and it praises.
screen: `THE HEAVENS DECLARE THE GLORY OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Find the sky you have, the night through a window, the daylight and clouds, or the last starry night you remember, and let your eyes go as far as they can; far beyond what you can see, Lemaître would say, the universe is still growing. If you pray, say the psalm's line, the heavens declare the glory of God; if not, simply look, and let yourself be small for a while.
Firmament. The King James word for the sky's dome, named in the psalm that watched beside Georges Lemaître's blackboard as he studied a universe with a beginning.
Your line: faith and science. One priest kept a blackboard and a prayer book both. Day nine hundred eighty-eight.

989.title: Mendel's peas
989.hook: an Augustinian friar in a monastery garden discovers the laws of heredity
989.howItsDone: Some religious orders, the Augustinians among them, keep gardens, schools and libraries alongside their life of prayer, and some of their members have worked as scientists.

segments.voice: Yesterday, firmament, a priest at a blackboard, and your line was faith and science.

Behind the walls of an abbey in Brno, in what is now the Czech Republic, there's a narrow strip of garden. A friar in a dark habit kneels in it with a small brush, moving pollen from one pea flower to another by hand, then tying a little bag over the flower so no bee can undo his work. He writes everything down. Tall plants, short plants. Smooth peas, wrinkled peas. Yellow, green. Season after season, he plants, crosses, counts and records. His brothers sing the hours in the chapel, and he walks back out to the rows. His name is Gregor Mendel.
screen: `A STRIP OF GARDEN BEHIND THE ABBEY.`

segments.voice: Mendel was an Augustinian friar, in a religious order that lives by a rule of prayer and shared life. His abbey valued learning, and sent him to study science. What he found in the garden: traits from the parent plants don't simply blend together like paint. Cross a tall pea with a short one, and the next generation can all come up tall. The shortness seems gone. But let those tall plants pollinate themselves, and in the next generation short ones come back. Something was being carried, hidden and passed on, in units that kept their identity from one generation to the next. Those units are now called genes, and their study genetics. Mendel had neither word. He had peas, patience and a notebook. His results drew little notice. He became abbot, busy running the house, and died before the world caught up. Later scientists found his paper and saw he had already worked it out in a garden. The Bible's first chapter has an old line about what he was watching, in the King James translation: "the herb yielding seed, and the fruit tree yielding fruit after his kind." Like gives rise to like. Genesis names the pattern; the friar counted how it works, row by row. Paul borrowed a gardener's picture too, writing about the church at Corinth: "I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase." The planter and the waterer do their part, and wait. Mendel's whole method was that kind of waiting.

If there's a plant near you, touch the soil and give it what it needs, water or light; if not, hold a seed or picture one in your palm, and think of everything packed into that small thing, waiting. You don't make it grow; you give it what it needs and wait. If you pray, say Paul's line, I have planted, but God gave the increase; if not, stay with the patience of it.
Mendel's peas. The garden experiments of Gregor Mendel, an Augustinian friar, which showed that traits are passed on in units that can hide and return.
Your line: the monk's garden. Some things only show up a generation later. See you tomorrow.

990.title: Bach's signature
990.hook: Bach signed his scores SDG, to God alone the glory
990.howItsDone: Some Christian musicians, artists and writers still mark their work with S.D.G. or soli Deo gloria, and others dedicate their work to God in a short prayer before they begin.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mendel's peas, a friar with a brush moving pollen between flowers, and your line was the monk's garden.

A church musician in Leipzig is up late, finishing a piece for Sunday. Choir parts, organ, strings, a hymn tune running through the middle of it all. He has a congregation to feed and a family to feed, and the deadline is days away, not months. He gets to the last bar, draws the final double line, and then, under the music, writes three letters. S. D. G. Not his name. Not a date. Three letters, where a signature would go. His name was Johann Sebastian Bach.

S. D. G. stands for three Latin words: soli Deo gloria. To God alone the glory. It's a short way of saying that the credit for any good thing belongs to God. Bach was a Lutheran, and he wrote it at the end of scores. At the top of some, he wrote two other letters, J. J., for Jesu juva: Jesus, help. Help at the start, glory at the end: the whole shape of a working day in four letters. The idea has a long echo in scripture. The opening of Psalm 115, in the King James Bible: "Not unto us, O LORD, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory." The psalmist says not unto us twice. It's hard to mean it the first time. And Paul takes the idea out of the church and into the kitchen: "Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God." Bach didn't save the letters for his grandest works. Tradition says he signed ordinary pieces too, written to a deadline for an ordinary Sunday. And some of his music for keyboard students, teaching pieces, carries a dedication along the same lines. The glory wasn't reserved for the masterpiece. It went on the homework. Bach could be stubborn, and he argued with his employers. The letters weren't a claim to be holy. They were a way of handing the work over when it was done.
screen: `SOLI DEO GLORIA: TO GOD ALONE THE GLORY.`

segments.voice: Pick one ordinary piece of work ahead of you, an email, a meal, a shift, a conversation with a child, and picture finishing it and quietly signing it, the way Bach signed his scores. If you pray, whisper S. D. G. at the end, or the psalm, not unto us, O Lord; if not, sign it for the person it serves, and let the credit go.

Your line: soli deo gloria. Even an ordinary Sunday piece got the letters. Day nine hundred ninety.

991.title: Rembrandt's prodigal
991.hook: an old painter paints the father's two different hands on his son's back
991.howItsDone: Some Christians meditate on paintings of Bible stories as a form of prayer, looking slowly at one image, and Rembrandt's prodigal son is a picture some return to again and again.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bach's signature, three letters under the last bar of a score, and your line was soli deo gloria.

Most of the canvas is dark. Brown, deep red, shadow. Out of it, light falls on two figures. A young man kneels with his back to the viewer, his head shaved, one shoe off, the other worn through at the heel. His face is pressed into an old man's chest. The old man bends over him, eyes half closed, his two hands resting on the young man's back. Off to the right, standing tall in a red cloak, another man watches, and doesn't come closer. Rembrandt painted this late in his life, art historians think, after years of loss.

The story is Jesus's, in the fifteenth chapter of Luke. A younger son takes his share of the inheritance, wastes it, ends up feeding pigs and hungry enough to want their food. He walks home with a speech ready. The King James Bible gives the moment: "But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him." The father runs before the son says a word. Rembrandt doesn't paint the running. He paints what comes after: the son home, the father holding him. Now look at the hands. Viewers have noticed they aren't a matching pair. One is broad and strong, the fingers spread, pressing. The other is slimmer and smoother, resting more gently. Some see a father's hand and a mother's hand. Some see firmness and tenderness together. Rembrandt left no note explaining them, so nobody knows for certain what he meant. And then there's the man in the red cloak. Viewers take him to be the elder brother, the one who stayed home and did everything right, and who in Luke's story stands outside, angry, refusing to come in. The father goes out to him too: "Son, thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine." The story ends with the father still speaking. Jesus never says whether the elder brother walked in. Rembrandt leaves him standing in the light, still deciding.
screen: `A GREAT WAY OFF, HIS FATHER RAN.`

Notice which figure your eye keeps returning to, without judging it. If you pray, rest in the line, his father saw him, and had compassion; if not, simply stay with the picture.

992.title: Handel's Messiah
992.hook: an oratorio sewn together from the King James Bible, first performed for charity in Dublin
992.howItsDone: Choirs and churches perform Messiah each year, especially around Christmas and Easter, and some cities hold sing-along performances where the audience joins the choruses.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rembrandt's prodigal, a dark canvas and a father's two hands, and your line was two hands.

A hall in Dublin, packed. The organizers have asked the ladies not to wear the wide hooped skirts of the day, and the gentlemen to leave their swords at home, so more people can squeeze in. The money from the tickets is going to charity. On the stage, singers and an orchestra, and a new piece by a German composer living in London, George Frideric Handel. No costume, no acting, no plot in the usual sense. Just singers and players and, word after word, the Bible.

Messiah is an oratorio: sacred words set to music for concert singers, without staging. Handel didn't write the words. A friend of his, Charles Jennens, assembled them, choosing rather than composing, from the King James Bible and the Prayer Book psalms. Isaiah's comfort ye. The shepherds in the fields. Behold the Lamb of God. I know that my redeemer liveth. It tells the whole story of Christ, from promise to birth to death to rising, using only scripture. At the close of the second section comes the Hallelujah chorus. Its words come from the book of Revelation. In the King James Bible, chapter nineteen: "Alleluia: for the Lord God omnipotent reigneth." Then, from chapter eleven, the line that gives today its carry: "The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord, and of his Christ; and he shall reign for ever and ever." Handel sets that last phrase so it comes round again and again, the voices overlapping, as if nobody can quite stop saying it. A custom goes with it. In some places, audiences stand for the Hallelujah chorus. Tradition says a king once stood at that moment, and everyone stood with him. There's no firm record that it happened. People stand anyway. What they're standing for is a line from the last book of the Bible: the kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord.
screen: `HE SHALL REIGN FOR EVER AND EVER.`

segments.voice: Play a recording of the Hallelujah chorus if you can, or read the two lines from Revelation slowly, and listen for the moment when he shall reign for ever and ever starts to repeat and overlap. If you pray, let it be your praise, and stand if you'd like to; if not, simply listen to an old, sung claim about whose kingdom lasts.

993.title: Mahalia Jackson
993.hook: the queen of gospel, who sang at the great civil rights march in the capital
993.howItsDone: Gospel music is sung in Black churches across the United States and far beyond, by choirs and soloists in Sunday worship, at funerals and at community gatherings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Handel's Messiah, a packed hall in Dublin, and your line was and he shall reign.

A crowd stretches down the National Mall, all the way along the reflecting pool. It's hot. Then a woman steps up to the microphones at the Lincoln Memorial, and she doesn't give a speech. She sings: an old spiritual about being scorned and put down, slow and huge, and the crowd goes still. A little later, Martin Luther King Jr. is speaking, and the story is told that she called out to him: tell them about the dream, Martin. However it happened, he moved away from his prepared text. Her name was Mahalia Jackson.

Mahalia Jackson grew up in New Orleans and sang in church from childhood. She moved north to Chicago and kept singing, in storefront churches, at funerals, anywhere they'd have her. Gospel music in that city was being shaped by people like Thomas A. Dorsey, a songwriter who had once played the blues. Dorsey wrote the song behind today's carry: Precious Lord, Take My Hand. By his own account, he wrote it out of grief, after his wife and newborn child died. It's a prayer from someone tired, barely standing, asking to be led home. She made it one of her signature songs. Offered good money to sing the blues, she turned it down; she would sing gospel and nothing else. The song's plea is an old one in scripture. In Isaiah, in the King James Bible, God says: "For I the LORD thy God will hold thy right hand, saying unto thee, Fear not; I will help thee." And in Psalm seventy-three, someone who has nearly lost their footing says: "Nevertheless I am continually with thee: thou hast holden me by my right hand." Hold my hand. A child says it crossing a street. When Martin Luther King Jr. was killed, Mahalia Jackson sang Precious Lord at his funeral. The movement that had marched to her singing now grieved to it. Gospel, the way she sang it, was never only for Sunday. It walked into the march and into the funeral, and kept asking for a hand.

Play Mahalia Jackson singing Precious Lord, Take My Hand, or any gospel recording you like, or read Isaiah's line slowly: I will hold thy right hand, fear not. Rest one hand open on your knee, and notice where in your life you'd like a hand to hold. If you pray, let the song carry your own asking; if not, let a woman singing for tired people keep you company.

994.title: Flannery O'Connor
994.hook: a Southern writer whose strange stories find grace in grotesque places
994.howItsDone: O'Connor's stories are read in classrooms, book groups and church study circles, where Christians talk about how grace can come through hard or strange moments.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mahalia Jackson, a woman singing at the Lincoln Memorial, and your line was precious lord.

A doctor's waiting room in the South. A respectable woman named Mrs. Turpin sits sizing everyone up: who's trashy, who's decent, who's beneath her. She's privately thanking Jesus that she was made the way she was. Across the room, a sullen college girl glares at her over a book. Then, without warning, the girl throws the book. It hits Mrs. Turpin in the face. The girl lunges at her, calls her an old wart hog and tells her to go back to hell. It's a scene from a short story called Revelation, funny and awful at once. The writer was Flannery O'Connor.

O'Connor spent her later years on a family farm in Georgia, raising peacocks and living with lupus, the illness that had taken her father. She was a devout Catholic, and she wrote stories full of con men, killers, prophets, and very proper people who are much less proper than they think. Her characters are often ugly, violent or ridiculous. Readers have asked why a writer of faith would write such grim, odd stories. Her answer, in her letters and essays, was that grace often arrives as a shock, and that her characters were too sure of themselves to notice it any other way. So the book in Mrs. Turpin's face isn't the end. That evening, hosing down her pigs, she argues with God out loud. Then she sees a procession stretching up into the sky, a vast crowd on its way to heaven. At the front, the people she looked down on, singing and leaping. At the back, people like her, decent and orderly, still singing on key, but with shocked faces, their virtues being burned away. Jesus told the respectable leaders of his day something like this. In Matthew, in the King James Bible: "the publicans and the harlots go into the kingdom of God before you." And Paul writes: "God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise." O'Connor's stories rarely end with anyone tidy. They end with someone struck, and seeing, maybe for the first time. Grace, in her fiction, doesn't knock politely. It throws the book.
screen: `A CATHOLIC WRITER ON A GEORGIA FARM.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who gets under your skin, not someone dangerous, just strange, awkward, hard to like, and look for one thing in them you missed: something they carry, something they do well, something they might be hoping for. If you pray, hold them before God just as they are; if not, let them be more than your first impression.
Flannery O'Connor. A Catholic writer from Georgia whose strange, often violent stories show grace breaking into the lives of people who are sure they don't need it.
Your line: grace in odd places. A week from a priest at a blackboard to a farm full of peacocks. Day nine hundred ninety-four.

fork.setup: you're Mrs. Turpin. a stranger has just thrown a book at you and called you an old wart hog and told you to go back to hell. that evening, alone with your pigs, what do you do?
options: forget it; she was clearly disturbed.
argue with God out loud about it.
call the girl's mother to complain.
fork.reveal: she argues with God, hosing down the pigs, and then sees a procession to heaven with the people she looked down on going first.

original.note: Greek: grace, an unearned gift — the word Paul uses for God's favor.

chat.says: Why would a devout Catholic write such violent, strange stories?
options: She believed grace often comes as a shock to people too sure of themselves.
She wanted to show that faith has nothing to say to ugly lives.
She wrote them before her faith, then stopped once she became devout.
chat.meaning: In her letters and essays, O'Connor said grace often arrives as a shock; her characters were too sure of themselves to notice it any other way.
